ch07.note: Su Shaoqing is retelling a story recorded of the Southern Tang court (see the note on Li Yu in Chapter 5). The younger Empress Zhou (小周后) was the sister, and later the second wife, of the Last Ruler Li Yu, who took her after the death of her elder sister, Empress Zhou the Elder. The anecdote — that the palace water-pavilions were lit not by lamps but by great pearls, whose glow filled the room like daylight — is the image behind this chapter’s title, ‘Pearls and Splendour’ (珠光宝气).

ch07.anchor: the Sunwatch Peak of Mount Tai
ch07.note: Mount Tai (泰山), in Shandong, is the easternmost and most revered of China’s five sacred mountains; emperors climbed it to offer sacrifice to Heaven. Watching the sun rise from its summit — here the ‘Sunwatch Peak’ (观日峰) — is a pilgrimage of long standing. Yan Tieshan’s disgust at having seen only ‘a great egg-yolk’ is a countryman’s joke against the whole solemn business.

Fen wine (汾酒), from Xinghua Village in Shanxi, is among the oldest and most celebrated of Chinese distilled spirits: a clear, dry, potent liquor of sorghum. That it is the wine of his own home province is a point of pride for the Shanxi-born Yan Tieshan.

ch07.anchor: the hearts that beat as one through a single thread
ch07.note: A line of the Tang poet Li Shangyin (李商隐, c.813–858): shen wu caifeng shuangfei yi, xin you lingxi yidian tong — ‘our bodies lack the bright phoenix’s paired wings, yet our hearts, through the one fine thread of the magic horn, beat as one.’ The lingxi was a rhinoceros horn anciently thought to hold a white filament along its length, a channel of secret sympathy. Famous as an image of lovers’ unspoken understanding, the line is borrowed here as the name of Lu Xiaofeng’s uncanny gift for reading an opponent’s next move; Huo Tianqing sets it beside Lu’s epithet ‘Twin Painted Wings’ (双飞彩翼), which plays on the poem’s opening line.

ch08.note: Chinese time-keeping here uses two old systems. The day was split into twelve shichen (时辰), ‘double-hours’ of two of our hours each, named for the zodiac animals; the hour of zi (子时) runs roughly from eleven at night to one in the morning. The night was further divided into five geng (更), ‘watches,’ each struck on a drum, so that the ‘third watch’ (三更, below) is the dead middle of the night. Three double-hours is thus about six of our hours.

The name echoes the Four Whitebeards of Mount Shang (商山四皓), four venerable sages who withdrew to that mountain amid the upheavals at the fall of the Qin (third century BC) and were later coaxed down to lend their prestige to the new Han dynasty. ‘The Heaven-Pine and the Cloud-Crane’ (天松, 云鹤) are the by-names of the two elders of this tale; pine and crane are both stock emblems of great age and of immortality.

ch08.anchor: a thing for throwing at dogs
ch08.note: A proverb: rou baozi da gou, you qu wu hui (肉包子打狗，有去无回), ‘throw a meat bun at a dog and it never comes back’ — said of anything paid out with no hope of return. The pedlar bends it into a grim jest, for his buns really are made to kill dogs.

ch08.anchor: these two words alone: honour and duty
ch08.note: Two set phrases close the letter. Mingri huanghua (明日黄花), ‘tomorrow’s chrysanthemums’ — here ‘the chrysanthemums of yesterday’ — is from the Song poet Su Shi: the chrysanthemum is the flower of the ninth-month festival, and the day after it is already out of season, so the phrase names a thing whose time has passed. Against that transience Huo Tianqing sets yiqi (义气), the two characters rendered ‘honour and duty’: the bond of loyalty and right dealing between men, which alone, he says, outlasts the ages.

ch08.anchor: an iron mace of eighty-three catties
ch08.note: Two feats of legendary loyalty. The man who ‘tattooed and disfigured himself and swallowed burning charcoal’ is Yu Rang (豫让) of the fifth century BC, who lacquered his skin to raise sores and swallowed charcoal to wreck his voice, all to get near and avenge his dead lord. The iron mace recalls the strong man whom Zhang Liang (张良) hired to hurl a great iron cone at the First Emperor of Qin at Bolangsha. Both are bywords for keeping faith unto death.

Dao yi you dao (盗亦有道), ‘even thieves have their Way’ — a phrase from the Zhuangzi, in which a robber-chief argues that thieving too has its code of wisdom, courage, and fair dealing. Lu Xiaofeng means that Sikong Zhaixing, thief though he is, keeps faith by rules of his own.
